blocks.title: Smog
blocks.text: Smog is a type of air pollution characterised by a thick haze. It occurs mainly in urban areas and is caused by emissions from vehicles, industry and other sources; it consists of fine dust or soot particles, condensed water vapour, poisonous gases such as SO2, NOx, O3, CO and CO2, secondary pollutants such as ozone, unburnt hydrocarbons, VOCs and particulate matter of 10 to 2.5 micrometres (Figure 14.3, smog around Lahore Fort).

There are two types. Classical or sulfurous smog, also called industrial, reducing or London smog, results from large quantities of sulfur oxides released into the air. Photochemical smog (Los Angeles smog) forms when primary pollutants such as nitrogen oxides, VOCs and unburnt hydrocarbons undergo photochemical reactions in sunlight to form secondary pollutants such as ozone and peroxyacetyl nitrates (PAN) (Figure 14.4); it is considered more dangerous, as it can cause heart palpitations, pneumonia and even lung cancer.

blocks.long_description: Classical smog is the reducing, sulfurous haze of coal-burning cities, while photochemical smog is the oxidising haze made when nitrogen oxides and volatile organics react in sunlight to give ozone and peroxyacetyl nitrate. Sulfur dioxide from fuels is oxidised to the trioxide and dissolves as sulfuric acid, and nitrogen dioxide gives nitric and nitrous acids, so rain with a pH below about 5 falls far downwind and corrodes buildings and ecosystems. The greenhouse effect arises because carbon dioxide, water vapour and other gases let short-wave sunlight through to warm the ground but absorb the long-wave heat the ground radiates back at night, so a rising concentration of these gases raises the global temperature. Burning fossil fuels and clearing forests are the human activities driving all of these.

blocks.prompt: Differentiate classical from photochemical smog, and say under what conditions photochemical smog forms (Quick Check 14.3a; exercise Q.2g; MCQ I, XII).
blocks.explanation: Classical smog is a reducing mixture of sulfur dioxide, soot and fog from burning coal, typical of cold, damp winter cities such as old London. Photochemical smog is oxidising: in strong sunlight nitrogen oxides and VOCs from traffic react to give ozone and PAN, so it forms on hot, sunny, still days in cities with heavy traffic; the brown colour comes from NO2 and its key marker is ozone with PAN.

items: Smog: thick urban haze of soot, water droplets, SO2, NOx, O3, CO, CO2, hydrocarbons, VOCs and PM10-2.5. Classical (London): SOx, reducing. Photochemical (Los Angeles): NOx + VOCs in sunlight give O3 and PAN; oxidising; more dangerous.
